product_name: RabbitAir MinusA2 Ultra Quiet HEPA Air Purifier - Stylish, Efficient and Energy Star (SPA-780A, Black, Germ Defense)
review_text:
I originally purchased the BigoGS 580 and found the sensors not reliable in my unit. The sensors went from green to red for no apparent reason if I moved it a foot. Instead of getting a replacement I switched to the MinusA2 Spa 700A (toxin remover) due to the 6 stage filtration. I live below two chain smokers and I want to ensure that I have the extra protection. I had the two units for about 2 days to 3 weeks so I can't comment on longevity.

It does a great job removing pollen and odor like the BioGS. It is pretty quiet. I don't even notice it on unless the room is completely silent. I noticed that the silent & quiet modes are more noticeable than the BioGS. I can hear the motor on the MinusA2 whereas on the BioGS I could not unless I was right next to it.

The only drawback that this unit has is if the room is dark, it automatically switches to sleep mode and turn off the sensor light. If you are living near smokers this does not work! Smoke could be drifting across my face and this unit does not adjust according to room condition. In order for it to do a thorough I have to leave it on low, med, high or turbo at night and this is not efficient use of energy.

Pros: Sleek, quiet, 6 stage filtration, option to turn off mood light, particle sensor, great customer service

Cons: lack of an odor sensor, black background make it tough to read the settings, auto mode not really 'auto' in the dark, cost of filters, bulky remote control

The only feature that this unit has that the BioGS doesn't is 2 extra stages of filtration. Is it worth the extra $60 to $140? The MinusA2 filters also cost more and need to be replaced more often. In my opinion, the BioGS is adequate if you are looking for a good air purifier.

product_name: AZEUS True HEPA Air Purifier | for HOME, for Large Room, Office or Commercial Space | Filter Pollen, Smoke, Dust, Pet Dander | Auto Mode | Air Quality Sensor | Night Light
review_text:
DISCLOSURE: This product was bought under another account, of which I live with that account holder. This review beholds my opinion, and none of which should be taken as scientific evidence (from a research firm).

Abstract: We bought this in the beginning of 2021, in hopes that it would greatly reduce the following in the living/dining room:

- The chances of transmitting the SARS-CoV-2 virus, known to cause COVID-19
- To reduce the prevalence of pet dander, dead skin cells and other dust particulates, therefore reducing the need to vacuum a fully carpeted area
- To control other VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds) and odours
- Explore different brand names that are not native to our country (United States)
- Overall satisfaction and durability of the product

The price as of the time was roughly $130 - $160, with included discounts on Amazon.

Results: While we haven’t been able to verify *if* this was able to slow or stop the transmission of any viruses in particular, we also aren’t confidently certain *if* it made any significant improvement over the following *several months* since we bought this product. However, observing the filter appears that it has been doing its job, but we haven’t noticed any observable difference in controlling odours—if there were any, at all. However, this product shows quite a plethora of issues that were not only mere oversights, but they were also egregiously condoned to be the norm as per the company’s (azeus’ or Azeus’) standards.

Details: First and foremost, we contacted their customer support after attempting to establish a warranty with them, which the product came with a pamphlet that claimed you can either get a free replacement filter (valued at $30 at least), or get a meagre $10 Amazon gift card. After uploading the screenshots as per their request, we opted for the free replacement filter. They, much to *our* surprise, *did not have any available on their end*. After some back-and-forth, we were left with no other option other than to allow them to give us a tiny return investment of $10 towards our Amazon gift card balance. We gave them the benefit of the doubt, since the supply chain during that time was severely affected, making availability on a *number* of products very scarce. How *that* came to pass was *also* just as peculiar: while I don’t know any intricacies involved, they ended up generating a gift card key/code at first, but the first one they gave turned out to be invalid or had already been used. So then they gave us another moments later, which that seemed to work. I don’t know if it took two or three attempts total to give us a working Amazon gift card code, but the way they went about it raised red flags to be quite honest: I thought all of this was purely shady business practises going on here. (I also want to note that I think they had an issue with us purchasing from an “unauthorised reseller” on Amazon, even though they were the *only choice on Amazon when we bought this air purifier*, which I think they used that as a reason to not honour either the warranty itself, or apply the warranty. Do not quote me on this one.)

Taking a look at their main website, it is an exceptionally sterile, web-only business website with no known physical location able to be found from the naked eye. Not a whole lot is given in the way of showing any modicum of legitimacy towards the average consumer. Perhaps it is a *new* way of starting up a business? But to not give *any* address besides an e-mail address, whatsoever, makes things feels either completely unfamiliar, or utterly suspicious. Every business we’ve dealt with so far already *has* an established address available for the public. And given the way the customer support speaks, they appear to be somewhere overseas. Not only that, but these icons they use to represent themselves appear more or less as if they used a stock photo that you could normally find on Google Images. That, or it coincidentally is also a professional shot for a business. It’s honestly unnerving, considering almost every business I came in contact with for a web chat practically had *nothing* like that.

Now back to the product, itself.

When we bought this, it was (at the time of purchase) rated to purify up to 560 sq. ft. to my recollection; we have a 500 sq. ft. combined living and dining room. But about 2 – 5 months later, the manufacturer seemingly updated their product page, *now claiming* to purify up to 1,080 sq. ft. rooms. This is seemingly more than *double* in comparison to the initial rating. Yet, we have no idea *how* they managed to make a relatively tiny device pull off that much. I think that’s *really suspicious*, to be frank. Also, it's worth mentioning that the original product page that we bought this air purifier from is no longer available, which is why I am reviewing it on this product's page.

When I examine the instruction manual, the fluency of English is at an acceptable state, noting some minor misspellings that most English-speakers would easily pick up, while there are some other unfamiliar phrasings used that is not widely accepted in the English language; again, this denotes that Azeus is *clearly* an overseas company that many can assume they are either from China, or somewhere within the “Middle East” (e.g. India). However, not *all* companies that use semi-fluent English originate *just* from these countries, either; other central European companies, such as “be quiet!” tends to not have the correct translation or phrasing of words translated from German to English at a similar rate. Though, the main issue tends to rear its ugly face, such as the feature of using the “ioniser”, which there is no real indication whether it is actually being used, and the UV bulb included in the product, which there is no indicator that it is—in fact—on, when you press the “UV” button. Interestingly enough, there is *no* button on the device for the UV bulb, either; it’s only unique to the remote. This is quite the massive oversight, indeed.

However, every time we turn it on without changing the fan speed, it operated in a rather foreign fashion where I had not expected an air purifier of *any* calibre to do what was known later a preset cycle that *always* occurs every time it is turned on. I’m not particularly impressed with the inanely loud noise the turbine fan produces when it is at its highest; I find this embarrassingly unbearable and it makes conversations more likely to be hard to follow, and it can be difficult for people to focus in mere silence. Therefore, as time went on, the fan speed is *always* set to medium. The featured, yet overly simplified air quality indicator is semi-consistent, where you may not always be certain if it is truly accurate. We have no idea how they managed to make it “sometimes” detect bacteria and viruses, yet consistently detect odours and fine particulates/dust, and frankly it would be very resourceful if consumers had access to that level of information.

When we used it for several months in total, we had not seen based on the instruction manual a “replace filter indicator” go off. In fact, the only thing that started to literally go off is the ioniser light, followed by the light for the selected fan speed on the device. This gives me even *far less confidence in this product* than they tried to let on, making me feel that, as my hunch dictated earlier, this was made to only be tossed out in the landfill after it met its very short-term use.

I also want to make one thing very clear: having a convectional air purifier, on paper, is a great concept. However, the intake on both sides of the product (on the smaller edges of this oval-shaped air purifier) *clearly* shows just how restrictive the overall air flow is. It is a neat concept that allows it to stay comfortably snug in very compact environments; it does *not*, however, make a very effective air purifier by not fully utilising the full surface area of the composite filter when it comes to pulling the “dirty air” in thru its intake vents. Ideally, it’s a great idea to have air go thru as little resistance as possible in order to make *any* fan-driven device extremely effective at its intended purpose. The fact that this is making air go through the equivalent to two 90° angles, followed by a multi-layered (yet also very expensive: at least or more than $30 per piece as of this writing) filter makes people like me syncope from such a ridiculous design.

Another note: I do think that the sleep mode functions as designed, noting that all lights go off after a brief period of time and reduces the fan speed at the lowest possible, making it virtually imperceptible while in operation. That’s a good plus. But! I don’t like how the lights, themselves, are unbearably bright: a light dimmer function would have been nice to have.

Overall impressions: They are generally **low**. I’m very uncertain on purchasing a new filter for this product, and I’m concerned that they are intentionally ripping their customers a new one. I have a higher probability of trying to find options provided by manufacturers such as Honeywell (brand owned by Kaz USA, Inc.) and GermGuardian (their entity, Guardian Technologies, is now acquired by Lasko, LLC as of January 2021: *also* an American manufacturer long known for their budget-oriented fans with high marks), which are well-known, well-established brands in the United States.

– End of review. Written on 30 November 2021, 1732 local time. –

review_title: Helps in reducing allergies but less than optimal for removing second-hand smoke!
review_text:
3-18-19 UPDATE COMMENT: I purchased the Rabbit Air Purifier directly from Rabbit Air two years ago and I attest it is a quality purifier compared to less expensive brands. The problem lies with replacement filters -- thus, if you reside around smokers, vapers, yearly wildfires, heavy street traffic you will need to replace the filters more often than the yearly recommendation. Several recent replacement filters I received have been inconsistent in their quality. My most recent order arrived with a leaky activated carbon filter (black dust in packaging and residue on my hands when touching the filter) and foul chemical odor in the HEPA and Odor filter that their customer service attributes to "off gassing". They sent me replacement filters but wanted photos of the filters I was returning. And to think, I was going to purchase a second air purifier from them. See the email from their customer service rep. Stay away from Rabbit Air and read the three star reviews as those reviews are right on!

Hi Christine,

Thank you for your email and I apologize that the exchange process became a hassle.

In trying to be thorough, it looks like it became more inconvenience than necessary. Per your request. we will cancel the shipment of the odor filter, but in the future, if it's ever needed, you are welcome to contact us again.

For the charcoal dust that you were concerned about, according to our researchers, we assume that there will be no health risks from the carbon dust. Due to the particle size, carbon dust is heavy, therefore, it would not become airborne easily. In addition, carbon dust could be very difficult to get into the body through the respiratory system even if it were to become airborne.

If you have any questions or if there is anything else that we can assist you with, please let us know.

Regards,

Tamina Park
Rabbit Air

Christine Carlino

7-19-2017 UPDATE COMMENT: After four months using the Rabbit Air Purifier in my 560 sq ft condo, I notice dust and small particle accumulation around the sides and bottom of the interior frame that holds the filters. For reference, I remove and clean the first filter that is washable and vacuum the four filters every other week. Unfortunately, this air purifier is no match for second hand cigarette smoke and marijuana odor from neighboring apartments. I purchased this filter because it does not off gas as many air filters do. I would not repurchase because of price. I'd recommend it for single family homes in controlling dust and light household odors, and those who are diligent in vacuuming and cleaning in general. Not optimal for attached condos or apartments in harsh environments.

ORIGINAL COMMENT: My allergist recommended this purifier to reduce allergens and help with second-hand smoke odors. I consider this to be a quality 5-filter purification system. For optimal results when I first received it, I ran the unit on Turbo or High for 72 hours in the bedroom and small living space to clear the air. I did not wake up with a stuffy noise and the air was fresher. Here is my analysis after a month:

Pros:
• Quality, solid craftsmanship. Stylish.
• Easy to read instructions and assemble right out of box.
• Air quality sensor light. Manually adjustable speed selection and auto mode.
• Removes airborne dust and particles in room size around 300 sq. ft or less.
• Good return policy and excellent customer service.
• Negligible ozone production.
• Manually adjustable speed selection and auto mode.

Cons:
• Pricey.
• The unit goes to 'sleep' in dark room, thus I run the system on manual low or medium at night to ensure the air is being filtered.
• Not good for older apartments or condos with leaky windows and doors.
• Detects and seems to eliminate kitchen / cooking smoke and odor but is less than optimal with reducing second-hand marijuana and tobacco odor (or smoke) from neighbors. The special “Odor” filter does not contain enough activated carbon to contain these odors.

NOTE: There is currently no air filter on the market that will “REMOVE” tobacco and weed smoke including the IQ Air Gas purifier. The IQAir has had issues with its V-5 Cell filter emitting foul odors.

review_title: Great Customer Service, Not so Great Air Purifier
review_text:
I bought the SPA-780A in Black with the Odor Remover Filter. I received it in November 2012 and promptly put it to work. I was looking forward to smoking a cigar inside a room in my home without the doors and windows open. It just didn't do the trick (i.e., remove the odors). After having a friend over and leaving the unit on Turbo for 4 days, the "next day smell of cigars" was still present. Now I like that smell. A good hint of vanilla & coffee from a good cigar. However, my wife doesn't like it. I called Rabbit Air and told them I would like to return the unit. They couldn't have been more pleasant. They were said they were surprised but that it doesn't work for everyone. They did say that some cigar bars in NYC use it with good results. Customer service suggested I give it another shot and put the unit closer to me. Well, I did, but it wouldn't have mattered if it was in my lap. It just didn't work. While putting together the unit I did notice the charcoal filter is very thin. It didn't seem like there was much charcoal at all. Now there are a bunch of other filters that go along with that so I guess that is their design.

In the end, I bought a set of new filters for my 10 year old Sharp Plasma Cluster. That unit comes with a thick charcoal bag type filter. It cleaned the room up in about 8 hours.

I will say that the Rabbit Air is a really good looking unit. There was no problem with them taking the unit back and refunding my credit card. I did have to pay $35 to send the unit back. I gave it 2 stars because the unit was really just 1 star but they had 5 star customer service. In the end though, I am buying the unit not their customer service. I am very happy with my old Sharp Plasma Cluster and will buy another Sharp when this eventually dies.
